FLUX LEVEL ANALYSIS The flux achievable at the NSTTF is closely related to the direct normal irradiance (DNI (W/m2)) at the site on the day of testing. The ability to confidently predict what seasons or months will have a consistently high DNI will enable staff at the NSTTF to schedule tests based on their desired flux; it is therefore important for past DNI and flux data to be recorded and analyzed with the goal of reducing test cancellations and unexpected decreases in flux levels. This section documents the analysis of past testing data from the solar tower, from year 2020 to 2025, including number of heliostats used, flux achieved, DNI, and solar tower level. Identification of consistently high DNI and flux results are outlined and necessary improvements to consistent data collection are highlighted. The data analyzed here includes all test records at the NSTTF Solar Tower One from 2020 to 2025, a total of 1122 data points. Most of these tests were not aiming for high flux (defined as 200-300 W/cm2 at the solar tower), and therefore most of the results achieve flux of less than 150 W/cm2. A DNI of greater than 850 W/m2 is considered a ‘good’ testing day at the NSTTF, and therefore most of the recorded data is from days where the DNI is above this threshold (Figure 6). Even from this Commented [RF1]: Link to figure 5 data, which is only recorded from days which were deemed high enough DNI to test, a yearly trend in DNI begins to emerge. January and February have the most consistently high DNI throughout the year, with a decrease beginning in March and continuing through August. Afternoon thunderstorms occur throughout the summer in New Mexico, accompanied by hazy atmospheric conditions which have a negative effect on the irradiance reaching the earth. In fall, DNI starts to increase once again, with November having a wide range of recorded DNI. Windy conditions also influence testing abilities, particularly in the spring – for instance out of 1122 data points analyzed, only 9 of those come from April (Figure 7).
